reference_title: Design, Analysis, and Testing of Laterally Loaded Deep Foundations that Support Transportation Facilities
chapter_title: Lateral Load Applications and Selection of Deep Foundation Type for Transportation Projects

sections.title: Lateral Load Applications for Transportation Projects
sections.summary: Heading for lateral load applications: typical applications for vertical deep foundations (2.1.1) and batter piles (2.1.2). The chapter gives an overview of laterally loaded deep foundations commonly used in transportation projects.
sections.body: This chapter provides an overview of laterally loaded deep foundations commonly used in transportation projects. Section 2.1 is the heading for typical lateral load applications for vertical deep foundations (2.1.1) and batter piles for lateral load applications (2.1.2); it has no text of its own. (p. 17)
sections.applicability: Transportation foundation applications where lateral loads are significant

sections.title: Typical Lateral Load Applications for Vertical Deep Foundations
sections.summary: Lateral loads come from braking, wind, waves and currents, debris and ice, thermal effects, vessel or vehicle impact, earth pressures, slope movements and earthquakes. Deep foundations resist them at bridge abutments and piers, excavation support, retaining walls, noise walls, slope stabilization and signs. Scour applies no load but adds unsupported length; liquefaction cuts resistance and may add lateral spreading load.
sections.body: Lateral loads in transportation projects can come from vehicle acceleration and braking on bridge decks and approaches; wind on traffic, bridge decks and structures; wave and current action on bridge piers; debris and ice floating in water courses; thermal effects (e.g., integral abutments); vessel/vehicle impact on piers and abutments; earth pressures behind abutment or retaining walls; slope movements; and seismic events. Lateral loads may be of comparable magnitude to axial loads. Deep foundations resist lateral loads at bridge abutments (Figure 2-1(a)), bridge piers (Figure 2-1(b)), temporary excavation support (Figure 2-2), permanent retaining walls (Figure 2-3), noise barrier walls (Figure 2-4), slope or landslide stabilization (Figure 2-5) and signs and traffic signals. Traffic, braking and wind forces act on a bridge pier along the longitudinal and transverse directions with the vertical loads (Figure 2-6); at abutments, lateral earth pressures are added to the loads from the structure. Pier foundations may be a single element such as a large diameter drilled shaft, or a group of piles, drilled shafts or micropiles. Earth pressures behind temporary and permanent retaining structures can be resisted by deep foundations: cantilever retaining walls may be pile supported like an abutment; cantilever or non-gravity walls can use soldier, secant or tangent piles, the retained earth load being carried by passive resistance of the embedded portion and the structural capacity of the piles; external braces or tieback anchors can be added for more capacity (printed "on-gravity wall systems"). Figure 2-7 suggests that a vertical element stabilizing a slope resists lateral loads above the potential slip surface and transfers them to the ground below; earth pressures above the slip surface are destabilizing and those below are stabilizing. For sound walls, traffic signals and signs, lateral loads are mostly from wind, typically resisted by a single drilled shaft (Figure 2-8) or occasionally a group of piles or small diameter shafts. Lateral loads can also come from vessel impact on fender systems (Figure 2-9), scour undermining bridge piers (Figure 2-10), and liquefaction or softening of soil layers around piers and abutments (p. 23). Where a fender system (dolphin or mooring system) is integral with a pier, vessel collision or mooring loads are transmitted to the foundation. In streams with high scour potential, foundations must extend sufficiently below the scour zone. Scour does not apply load directly, but scour on one side or around the foundation causes unbalanced earth pressures and/or additional moments from the increased unsupported length. Seismic lateral loads can be much larger than static because of structural inertia forces and the possible loss of resistance if liquefaction occurs; liquefaction reduces the lateral resistance and may increase demand through lateral spreading or flow of the ground above the liquefied layer. (pp. 17 to 24)
key_points: Sources: braking, wind, waves and currents, debris and ice, thermal effects, impact, earth pressure, slope movement, earthquakes (p. 17).
Applications: abutments, piers, excavation support, retaining walls, noise walls, slope stabilization, signs (p. 17).
Slope stabilization: load above the slip surface is carried into the ground below it (p. 17).
Scour applies no load directly but increases unsupported length and moments (p. 23).
Liquefaction reduces lateral resistance and may add lateral spreading or flow loads (p. 23).

sections.title: Batter Piles for Lateral Load Applications
sections.summary: Batter piles (typically 1H:12V to 1H:3V) resist lateral load mainly through the horizontal component of their axial load; micropiles in A-frame configurations stabilize slopes. Batter piles give less displacement, often with fewer piles, but are discouraged in seismic areas (poor ductility, abrupt shear failure, greater demand) and where the overlying soil may settle significantly.
sections.body: Most applications discussed are for vertical (plumb) elements, but batter piles can also resist lateral loads. They are installed at a batter that typically varies from 1H:12V to 1H:3V and resist lateral loads primarily through the horizontal component of the axial load, as set by the batter angle, whereas vertical piles resist primarily through structural shear and bending. Bending of batter piles also contributes, particularly at small batter angles. The axial resistance can be in compression or tension. Typical applications are two or more rows of driven piles for bridge foundations with batter piles in one or more rows (see Figure 2-9). Micropiles can be battered for similar applications and for slope stabilization with one or more rows at different batter angles (Figure 2-11); in this "A-frame" configuration they resist the sliding forces through axial compression, tension and shear. Plumb piles are commonly used because they are easier and less costly to construct; batter piles typically give the necessary resistance with less displacement and often with a smaller group (p. 25). In recent years batter piles have been discouraged in seismic areas or where a ductile response is needed: they have performed relatively poorly in earthquakes from lack of ductility in compression and tend to fail abruptly in shear (Ferritto et al. 1999), and as a stiffer foundation they can draw greater lateral demand; where used in seismically active areas, the increased stiffness must be accounted for in design. They are also typically discouraged where overlying soil is expected to settle significantly relative to the foundation. (pp. 24 to 25)
key_points: Batter typically 1H:12V to 1H:3V; resistance mainly from the horizontal component of axial load (p. 24).
Battered micropiles in A-frame configuration stabilize slopes (Figure 2-11) (p. 24).
Batter piles give less displacement, often with a smaller group (p. 25).
Discouraged in seismic areas: poor ductility in compression, abrupt shear failure, greater demand (Ferritto et al. 1999) (p. 25).
Also discouraged where overlying soil will settle significantly relative to the foundation (p. 25).

sections.title: Types of Deep Foundations Addressed in This Manual
sections.summary: Significant lateral forces and moments need sections with adequate bending and shear resistance, so most applications use piles or drilled shafts; micropiles and CFA piles (with casing or reinforcing) serve when lateral loads are not significant. Not addressed: vibro-compacted concrete columns, unreinforced auger-cast piles, helical and timber piles.
sections.body: Lateral load applications typically involve significant lateral forces and/or moments, producing significant internal bending moments and shear forces; design for them requires deep foundations with adequate structural section and bending moment resistance, so most applications use piles or drilled shafts. Micropiles and CFA piles, especially with permanent steel casings (for micropiles) and internal reinforcing, can also resist lateral loads, especially if the lateral loads are not significant; micropiles can also be battered (Section 2.1.2). The document focuses mostly on piles and drilled shafts as the most common types. Systems not addressed are those with limited tension or moment capacity, such as vibro-compacted concrete columns and unreinforced auger-cast piles, and those not typically used in transportation facilities, such as helical piles and timber piles. In summary, the types addressed are driven piles, drilled shafts, micropiles and continuous flight auger (CFA) piles. (p. 25)
key_points: Types addressed: driven piles, drilled shafts, micropiles, CFA piles (p. 25).
Most lateral applications use piles or drilled shafts for bending and shear resistance (p. 25).
Micropiles and CFA piles suit lateral loads that are not significant, with casing or reinforcing (p. 25).
Not addressed: vibro-compacted concrete columns, unreinforced auger-cast, helical and timber piles (p. 25).

sections.title: Selection of Deep Foundation Types for Resistance of Lateral Loads
sections.summary: Shallow foundations are considered first; deep foundations are preferred for no competent stratum at economical depth, footing size, excessive settlement, significant uplift or lateral loads, scour or liquefaction, and when overturning dominates. Factors for selection: subsurface conditions, design loads, scour or liquefaction, element properties, constructability, cost, redundancy, acceptable lateral displacement and local experience.
sections.body: Selecting the optimum foundation first considers whether shallow foundations are better alternatives; they are typically more economical, less complex and easier to construct. Deep foundations are preferred or required when a competent stratum is not within an economical depth, when the required footing dimensions cannot be accommodated, when settlement is excessive, when significant uplift or lateral loads are present, and when the bearing support may be subject to scour or liquefaction. Foundation types are evaluated on vertical loads and settlement and on lateral resistance and displacement; vertical loads, axial capacity and settlement are beyond this document, which focuses on selection when lateral loads are significant or controlling. Shallow foundations offer only limited lateral capacity, from passive resistance on the side and/or shear along the base. Deep foundations develop high lateral resistance over their depth, are generally more economical when overturning loads dominate (noise barrier walls, sign posts), and can intercept a slope failure plane and develop resistance below it. The factors in selecting deep foundations to resist lateral loads are: subsurface conditions and geomaterial properties; design loads; potential for scour or liquefaction; structural properties of the elements; constructability; cost-effectiveness; structural redundancy; and acceptable magnitude of lateral displacement. Availability of local experience and construction practices may also be a factor. These factors are discussed in the following subsections. (p. 26)
key_points: Consider shallow foundations first; they are usually cheaper and simpler (p. 26).
Deep foundations suit large lateral or overturning loads, scour, liquefaction or no competent shallow stratum (p. 26).
Selection factors: ground, loads, scour/liquefaction, element properties, constructability, cost, redundancy, displacement (p. 26).

sections.title: Subsurface Conditions and Geomaterial Properties
sections.summary: Subsurface factors: hard or soft strata setting tip elevations, soft soils and fill at shallow depth (which govern lateral soil resistance), depth to rock and groundwater. Geomaterial properties must be established by field and laboratory testing (AASHTO, Mayne et al. 2002, Loehr et al. 2016); Chapter 3 gives the parameters.
sections.body: Subsurface conditions that specifically affect the selection of deep foundations for lateral loads include the occurrence and distribution of hard or soft strata (for the range of pile/shaft tip elevations), soft soils and fill at shallow depth that have a major influence on available lateral soil resistance, depth to rock, and groundwater levels. Since lateral resistance depends on the engineering properties of the geomaterials, these must be adequately established from field and laboratory testing. Guidelines for subsurface investigations are in the AASHTO LRFD specifications, Mayne et al. (2002), Loehr et al. (2016) and local standards; Chapter 3 gives the engineering properties needed to analyze deep foundations under lateral loads. (p. 26)
key_points: Soft soils and fill at shallow depth strongly influence available lateral resistance (p. 26).
Hard or soft strata, depth to rock and groundwater also govern selection (p. 26).
Properties must come from field and laboratory testing; see Chapter 3 (p. 26).

sections.title: Properties of Deep Foundation Elements
sections.summary: Elements with large bending stiffness resist horizontal loads with smaller deformation; orient H-piles for one-way loads, consider batter elements, and prefer ductile steel H or pipe piles for large dynamic or cyclic loads. Where lateral loads are significant, shear and bending typically govern pile and shaft size, except with batter piles.
sections.body: Piles or shafts with relatively large bending stiffness are more suitable for horizontal loads because structural resistance is mobilized with smaller deformation. If horizontal loads act mainly in one direction, elements stiffer in one direction (such as steel H-piles) must be oriented to resist the primary loading. Batter elements may add significant lateral resistance without increasing the number of elements. If large dynamic or cyclic loads are anticipated, a ductile material such as steel H-piles or pipe piles may be preferred. Structural resistances (compression, tension, shear, bending, buckling) depend on the material (timber, steel or concrete) and the cross section. Where applied lateral loads are significant, shear and bending moment typically govern the size of both piles and drilled shafts, except when batter piles are used. (p. 27)
key_points: Large bending stiffness mobilizes resistance with smaller deformation (p. 27).
Orient H-piles to the primary load direction; ductile steel piles for large dynamic or cyclic loads (p. 27).
Shear and bending typically govern size where lateral loads are significant, except batter piles (p. 27).

sections.title: Constructability Considerations
sections.summary: A design that cannot be built to the required depth or size cannot give the required lateral resistance, so constructability and its cost enter type selection: site access and space, local practice and contractors; obstructions, depth to rock, groundwater, contamination; drivability, tooling, installation time, testing and inspection; noise, vibration and disturbance of adjacent ground.
sections.body: Constructability must be addressed during design: if the foundation cannot be installed to the required depth or size, the required lateral resistance may not be achieved, so constructability and the cost of overcoming construction challenges must be considered in selecting the type. General constructability: site access for the large cranes needed for pile driving or large drilled shafts (smaller elements if access is an issue; micropiles may be the only feasible type on small sites or with limited headroom); space for a pile or shaft group and cap (otherwise a single large diameter shaft); local practice or precedent, some DOTs preferring certain elements; and experience of local contractors, notably for micropiles and large diameter drilled shafts. Subsurface conditions: hard layers or obstructions may make driven piles impractical (drilled shafts or micropiles can penetrate them); laterally loaded elements need a minimum embedment that may require penetrating shallow rock, which driven piles and CFA piles may not reach; high groundwater, artesian conditions or flowing or running sands can be an issue for drilled shafts (p. 28), where driven piles may be more appropriate; contaminated soils favor driven piles, which make no spoils, while drilled shafts, micropiles and CFA piles require disposal of contaminated spoils. Installation: drivability to the required tip elevations must be evaluated in design, piles needing capacity to overcome driving resistance and stiffness and strength to withstand driving without damage (a drivability assessment is recommended in AASHTO 2014); drilled shafts may need tool changes for hard layers, obstructions or rock, and casing, casing oscillators, slurry and a slurry plant should be assessed; installation time varies by type (e.g., CFA groups may be preferred to driven piles or small shafts for faster production, if axial capacity is not an issue); construction testing (drilled shafts may need integrity testing such as CSL, axial and lateral load tests; lateral testing is easier on an individual pile of a group design than on large shafts); and inspection (pile driving inspection is relatively simple; slurry shafts may need specialized techniques for alignment, bottom clean out and concrete placement). Effects on nearby structures or public perception: noise and vibration from pile driving, and from downhole hammers or drop chisels for rock sockets in urban settings, and impacts on marine environments; driving can densify, displace or heave adjacent ground and structures (low-displacement H-piles or pre-drilling reduce this), post-driving consolidation of cohesive soils may occur as excess pore pressures dissipate, and vibratory casing installation may densify and settle adjacent ground. Further details: Hannigan et al. (2016) for driven piles, Brown et al. (2010) for drilled shafts, Brown et al. (2007) for CFA piles and Sabatini et al. (2005) for micropiles (p. 29). (pp. 27 to 29)
key_points: An unbuildable design may not achieve the required lateral resistance (p. 27).
Micropiles may be the only feasible type on small sites or with limited headroom (p. 27).
Obstructions and shallow rock may rule out driven or CFA piles; groundwater may hamper drilled shafts (pp. 27 to 28).
Contaminated soils favor driven piles, which produce no spoils (p. 28).
Consider drivability, tooling, installation time, testing, inspection, noise, vibration and ground disturbance (p. 28).

sections.title: Cost Effectiveness
sections.summary: Cost analysis is recommended, especially when alternatives perform comparably: mobilization, materials, installation, local practice and restrictions, delays, load testing, number of elements and cap. Driven piles are individually cheaper, but fewer drilled shafts may replace many piles; a single large shaft can eliminate a group and cap; driven piles often suit small single-span bridges.
sections.body: A cost analysis is recommended when selecting among deep foundation types for lateral resistance, particularly when the alternatives perform comparably, and should consider all aspects of the design: constructability, seismic design, structural connections and temporary works can significantly affect cost, and failing to consider them may raise final costs or lead to a foundation that is not the most economical; overly conservative designs and inappropriate construction practices may also raise cost significantly. It should include mobilization, materials, installation, locally available practices, local restrictions (permits, time-of-year), potential delays, load testing programs, the total number of piles/shafts, the pile/shaft cap and other factors. Cost-efficiency can be analyzed as total cost per foundation unit or as unit cost per linear foot along a wall or slope. Individual driven piles are generally less costly than individual drilled shafts, but drilled shafts often have higher axial and lateral resistance so fewer can replace more piles. For small single-span bridges needing some lateral resistance, driven piles are often more economical; for piers of large bridges, more piles and a larger cap would be needed than for a group of drilled shafts, and a single large diameter shaft can eliminate a pile group and cap. Batter piles may have some cost and lateral resistance advantages compared to drilled shafts. Cost analysis is a broad topic covering axial and structural design too, such as axial load test costs, and construction duration may affect the schedule and cost. (p. 29)
key_points: Recommended when alternatives perform comparably; include all design and construction factors (p. 29).
Express as total cost per unit or cost per linear foot of wall or slope (p. 29).
Driven piles are individually cheaper; a single large shaft can eliminate a pile group and cap (p. 29).

sections.title: Redundancy of the Foundation System
sections.summary: Pile/shaft groups may be redundant depending on layout and number, others carrying a failed element's load subject to group effects; a single-element foundation is non-redundant, so replacing a group with one shaft loses redundancy. Redundancy matters more axially than laterally and is addressed by LRFD resistance factors (Chapter 4).
sections.body: Structural redundancy may provide adequate support if individual elements fail, or the lack of it should be considered in design. Pile/shaft groups may be considered redundant depending on the layout and if there are enough elements; if one fails, the others may overcome the deficiency, although the ability to transfer its load to the other elements is related to group effects. Deep foundations of a single element are non-redundant (p. 30), so when a single drilled shaft replaces a number of driven piles or smaller shafts, the group's redundancy is lost. Redundancy is typically more significant for axial than for lateral capacity, and is typically addressed by resistance factors in the LRFD platform (Chapter 4). (pp. 29 to 30)
key_points: Groups may be redundant, subject to layout, number and group effects (p. 29).
Single-element foundations are non-redundant (p. 30).
Redundancy is addressed by LRFD resistance factors (Chapter 4) (p. 30).

sections.title: Exclusions
sections.summary: Not addressed: elements with little lateral capacity (unreinforced CFA, vibro concrete columns), specialty or uncommon foundations (helical and screw piles), continuous cantilevered walls (sheetpile, secant and tangent pile walls, analysed differently), and systems with external lateral support such as anchored or braced piles.
sections.body: Deep foundation elements with little lateral capacity, such as unreinforced CFAs or vibro concrete columns, are not addressed, nor are specialty foundations or those not common for U.S. transportation projects, such as helical piles, screw piles and similar types. The document is not applicable to continuous cantilevered retaining walls, such as sheetpile, secant pile or tangent pile walls, because the methods for continuous walls differ from those for individual or groups of laterally loaded deep foundations. More complex systems using external supports for lateral resistance, such as anchored piles or braced piles, are also not addressed. (p. 30)
key_points: Not addressed: unreinforced CFA, vibro concrete columns, helical and screw piles (p. 30).
Not applicable to continuous walls: sheetpile, secant pile, tangent pile walls (p. 30).
Anchored or braced pile systems are not addressed (p. 30).
